title: MTA Operating Budget Outlook: Short-Term Stability, Long-Term Risks
plain_title: MTA budget is balanced now but has a bigger underlying gap
what_they_audited: A Citizens Budget Commission report reviewing the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's (MTA's) November 2025 Financial Plan and its outlook through 2029.
background: The plan is balanced in 2025 and 2026 and reports gaps of $160 million in 2027, $243 million in 2028 and $306 million in 2029.

findings.plain: The difference between the MTA's recurring revenues and recurring expenses is much larger than the gaps the plan reports.
findings.quote: the MTA’s underlying structural budget gap—the difference between recurring revenues and recurring expenses—is substantially larger, reaching $1.1 billion in 2029

findings.plain: The multi-year plan leans on one-time money, including federal disaster reimbursements and casino license fees.
findings.quote: the multi-year plan relies on $2.1 billion in one-time resources, including Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) reimbursements and downstate casino license fees

findings.plain: The MTA's finances have improved substantially compared with the outlook three years earlier.
findings.quote: The MTA’s financial position has improved significantly since the November 2022 Financial Plan projected a $1.6 billion deficit for 2026.

findings.plain: The plan counts on newly identified operating efficiencies by the end of the decade.
findings.quote: newly-planned operating efficiencies anticipated to save $250 million per year by 2029

findings.plain: Labor costs are a risk because negotiated raises could come in above the plan's assumption.
findings.quote: Collectively-bargained annual raises could exceed the 2 percent assumed in the plan.

findings.plain: Fare evasion continues to drain revenue from the operating budget.
findings.quote: Continue to reduce fare evasion, which is on track to cost more than $900 million this year

numbers.label: One-time resources in the multi-year plan
Projected cost of fare evasion this year

recommendations: Put in place more operating efficiencies with labor by changing work rules, increasing employee availability and sharing the benefits of higher productivity.

Keep reducing fare evasion by assessing the cost-effectiveness of enforcement, refining the multifaceted approach, accelerating new faregates and proof-of-payment and working with the district attorneys on serial cases.
Work with the city to improve enrollment in Fair Fares NYC, assess its cost-effectiveness and consider expanding it.
Reduce paratransit costs per trip by using the fleet and broker services strategically and considering more shared rides.
Continue biennial fare and toll increases and consider tying them to year-over-year expense growth instead of a flat 4 percent.
